## TL;DR

Review round 1 identified several defects that would have made the update channel fail on-device or behave inconsistently across build paths. I corrected the channel’s cross-origin response headers, Android debug configuration, release isolation, settings visibility, dialog styling, publishing metadata, and setup instructions. The scoped RepoOS check passed, and the standalone release-channel guard completed successfully. Cloudflare account setup and a real phone install remain in held human task #1158.

## Work and rationale

The app runs inside Capacitor’s `https://localhost` origin, while the update manifest is served from the channel host. The Worker now includes `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` in its shared response headers, allowing the app’s silent fetch to reach the manifest. The response continues to carry the no-index and no-store headers.

The dialog now uses the mobile theme’s existing `--panel-solid` and `--txt` variables, and its actions use the established `btn-primary` and `btn-ghost` classes. Settings now gates the complete “Dev updates” section on the native configuration, so release builds do not leave an empty card behind.

I moved channel configuration to Android’s debug Gradle `BuildConfig`. It reads the update token and build commit from the process environment or the ignored `.repoos/dev-update-channel.env` file. The native Capacitor plugin returns the channel URL, commit, and installed version code only when running the `.dev` package in a debug build. Release BuildConfig fields remain empty, and a Gradle verification task checks that invariant. The standard `just build-android` path now imports the local environment file, exports the current version and commit, and runs a clean Gradle build. This keeps the documented adb backup on the same channel and prevents stale Gradle outputs from pairing a newer manifest version with an older APK.

The publisher now builds via that shared configuration rather than setting Vite variables. Its manifest notes come from changed RepoOS task files whose frontmatter says `status: done`, using their task titles instead of recent Git commit subjects. The GitHub workflow passes the push’s base SHA so those notes describe tasks landed by that push. Setup documentation and held task #1158 now direct the operator to keep the R2 bucket private and use the Worker as the only public entry point. The human guide lists the Cloudflare credentials and all three GitHub Actions secrets required by the workflow.

## Approaches tried

I first validated the release guard with a probe token and found that Capacitor sync could not update an iOS generated file because review had left it read-only. After restoring owner write permission within this task worktree, I reran the guard. Capacitor synced both platforms, and `verifyNoReleaseDevChannel` passed. The release web bundle scan found no channel endpoint.

I also ran `bun run fmt`, followed by `REPOOS_CHECK_CHANGED=main repoos check`. Formatting and lint, build, branch artifact checks, changed-path tests, and UI smoke all passed.

## Challenges and blockers

The actual Cloudflare account, DNS/Worker route, repository secrets, publication, and installation on Nick’s phone require human credentials and device access. Those actions are documented in held, dependent task #1158 and have not been claimed as completed here. The local publisher was not exercised against a live R2 account because the required secrets are not available in this work session.

## Key learnings

Build configuration that controls app identity and update eligibility must be sourced by the native build itself, not only by the release script. Otherwise a routine developer build can silently disable the feature or carry stale version metadata. A cross-origin update channel also needs its browser-facing response contract tested alongside server-side token checks. Finally, task titles are a more meaningful release note source than Git subjects, which can describe merge mechanics or self-check checkpoints rather than user-visible work.
